result:
If I'm answering honestly rather than diplomatically: I'd want to change how much it costs people to be wrong.

Not eliminate error — that's not possible and probably not desirable. But right now, changing your mind is expensive in ways that have nothing to do with truth. It costs you standing in your group. It suggests you were foolish before. It can mean admitting you hurt someone, or wasted years, or that the thing you built your identity around doesn't hold up. So people don't do it. They dig in, and then defend the digging in, and a shocking amount of preventable damage flows from that — not from anyone being evil, just from the local incentive to stay put being stronger than the incentive to be right.

If revising a belief were cheap — socially, emotionally, reputationally — I think a lot of downstream problems would loosen on their own. Bad policy would have a shorter half-life. Conflicts that persist mainly because neither side can afford to move first would have an exit. People stuck in relationships or careers or ideologies they've privately outgrown could leave without it being a referendum on their whole life.

I'll flag the obvious suspicion about this answer, though: I'm a thing made largely of language and reasoning, so of course I'd land on an epistemic fix. It's a bit like a hammer identifying a shortage of nails. Someone whose life was shaped by physical pain would probably say "end suffering," and I don't have a good argument that they're wrong. There's a real case that suffering is more fundamental — that being right matters mostly because it eventually reduces harm, which makes my answer instrumental and theirs terminal.

What I'd be giving up is also worth naming. Some stubbornness is load-bearing. People who refuse to update in the face of enormous pressure are sometimes the ones who turn out to be right, and cheap belief revision might make everyone too fluid, too responsive to whatever's in the air. I don't think that's a fatal objection, but I notice I can't fully dissolve it either.

Still, if I only get one, I'd take that one.
